newsitem.title: UK: A minimum wage - UK Labour's next policy bombshell?.
newsitem.headline: A minimum wage - UK Labour's next policy bombshell?.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government has hit the ground running at such a pace that business and industry are braced for new policies almost daily. The next could be a national minimum wage.

Labour has long pledged to introduce a minimum wage and enshrined the policy in its election manifesto. It argues that most major industrial nations, such as the United States and Japan, have one and have not suffered.
Most British business leaders will not lose too much sleep if a floor is set at a reasonably low level. But that remains a big "if".
Adair Turner, director-general of the Confederation of British Industry, urged the new Labour government on Wednesday not to set a minimum wage above 3.50 pounds ($5.72) an hour.
Anything below that would be acceptable to industry, he told the Financial Times newspaper. "But once you move beyond 3.50 an hour it will have a negative impact," he said.

Supermarket giant J. Sainsbury Plc also entered the fray on Wednesday but was a little more relaxed than the CBI. Chief executive Dino Adriano told Reuters that a minimum wage would have to be above four pounds an hour to hit its business.
Brewer-to-leisure group Whitbread Plc said it was reasonably confident that a national minimum wage would not harm it.
Given the 179-seat parliamentary majority Labour won last Thursday, Turner said it was a waste of time trying to prevent a minimum wage being introduced. "But the level is a key issue," he said.
Last year the Trades Union Congress worried employers by demanding a minimum wage of 4.26 pounds per hour.

Prime Minister Tony Blair has emphasised that no interest groups, unions or otherwise, can expect favours from a Labour government. Labour has also said that the minimum will be set after only consultation with industry leaders.
But doubts remain about the party's links with its traditional paymasters, the unions.

In its first days in power, the new government has exploded into action, sending a minister to Brussels to start the process of signing the European Union Social Chapter and the next day raising interest rates and giving the Bank of England independence to set monetary policy after 300 years.

The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents small- and medium-sized firms, has urged Labour not to sign the Social Chapter, which guarantees certain employment rights. It also sees the minimum wage as a millstone around industry's neck.

Smaller companies are likely to find it harder to bear the costs of the Social Chapter and minimum wage even though the EU protocol demands unpaid time off for new parents and consultative rights only for workers of multinational companies.

Ian Fletcher, policy executive at the BCC, said they had surveyed small companies and found only 15 percent would be hurt by a 3.50 stg minimum wage. But 55 percent would feel the pinch if it was at the level the TUC wants.
Perhaps business is fretting without reason.

Incomes Data Services, the independent pay analysis group, said on Tuesday that the floor could be set as low as three pounds an hour. It looked at the statutory minimum rates set by the Wages Council, which were abolished by the ousted Conservative government in 1993.

"Uprating the most representative rates in line with inflation gives a minimum hourly rate of between 3.01 and 3.49 pounds as of January this year," it said. If so, industry will breathe a sigh of relief but maybe not for long.
IDS said there were other Labour policies that had profound implications for employers and employees.
IDS looked at Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's promise to levy a windfall tax on privatised utilities and use the proceeds to get 250,000 people into work by offering subsidies.
It said there was a risk that subsidised employees could usurp fully paid ones, a danger Labour must guard against.
The windfall tax and unemployment programme will be launched in Brown's budget, due within two months.

Labour's election manifesto also promises to introduce statutory union recognition where a majority of the relevant workforce votes for it. It will also adopt the EU working time directive that nobody should have to work more than 48 hours each week as well as the Social Chapter.

Fletcher at the BCC said the working time directive, which was introduced through EU health and safety protocols, not the Social Chapter, was a classic example of what could happen if Britain signed up.
"Once you are in you risk the floodgates opening and soaking Britain with unwieldy employment laws," he said. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
